gloss_terse: cover, overlay, panel with boards or planks (especially in construction)
gloss_readable: This rare Hebrew root appears in the context of Solomon's temple construction, describing the covering or paneling of the building's interior structure. The single biblical occurrence speaks of covering the house with beams, suggesting a process of adding an upper layer or ceiling. The cognate evidence from Phoenician (roof), Aramaic (be covered/overlaid), and Akkadian (cover, overwhelm) confirms the semantic range of concealment or overlaying with protective or decorative materials.

senses.1: The multilingual evidence shows some uncertainty in how to render this technical architectural term, with translations ranging from 'hidden treasures' (likely a misunderstanding of the context) to more general covering concepts. The placement in Deuteronomy 33:19 suggests the translators struggled with a rare word, though the temple-construction context in 1 Kings 6:9 more clearly supports the sense of paneling or beaming a structure.

gloss_terse: abundance, fullness, plenty (especially of natural resources)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes material abundance or plenty, appearing in Moses' blessing upon the tribes in Deuteronomy 33:19. In context, it refers to the abundant resources—treasures hidden in the sand—that Zebulun and Issachar would enjoy. The word captures the idea of overflowing provision, whether from the sea's riches or the land's productivity. It conveys the sense of more than enough, a superabundance that goes beyond mere sufficiency.

senses.1: The consistent cross-linguistic rendering as 'abundance' or 'fullness' (Spanish abundancia, French abundance, German Fülle) confirms this is a straightforward term for plenty or bounty. The context in Deuteronomy 33:19 links this abundance specifically to the 'hidden treasures of the sand,' suggesting maritime wealth or mineral resources available to these coastal and inland tribes.

gloss_terse: Shiphi (personal name of a Simeonite clan leader)
gloss_readable: Shiphi appears as a personal name in the genealogical records of the tribe of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4:37. The name belongs to one of the ancestral heads whose descendants grew numerous during the reign of Hezekiah. Like many biblical names, it likely carries theological or descriptive significance, though its precise etymology is uncertain. The Greek transliterations (Sepei, Sophei) show slight variation in vocalization.

senses.1: Most modern translations simply transliterate the Hebrew name as 'Shiphi' or 'Siphi,' while some French and German versions leave it untranslated in Hebrew characters. The name occurs in a genealogical context listing the leaders of Simeonite clans who experienced population growth and territorial expansion in the days of Hezekiah.

gloss_terse: be beautiful, fair, pleasing, or comely
gloss_readable: This Hebrew verb expresses aesthetic and emotional satisfaction, describing something that is visually beautiful or personally pleasing. The single occurrence in Psalm 16:6 uses an Aramaism to describe the psalmist's inheritance as 'beautiful' or 'pleasing' to him. The root connects to the broader Semitic family where similar forms convey brightness, beauty, or the removal of a veil to reveal attractiveness. It captures both objective beauty and subjective pleasure in what one possesses or experiences.

senses.1: The multilingual glosses consistently render this as 'beautiful,' 'fair,' or 'pleasing' (Spanish hermosa, French beau, German schön), confirming the aesthetic-evaluative sense. In Psalm 16:6, the psalmist declares that his 'heritage is beautiful to me,' expressing deep satisfaction with God's apportionment of his life—a fitting conclusion to the declaration that 'the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places.'

gloss_terse: beauty, goodliness, attractiveness
gloss_readable: This noun denotes beauty or attractive appearance, occurring in Jacob's blessing upon Naphtali in Genesis 49:21. The phrase 'words of beauty' (or 'beautiful words') is part of the poetic imagery describing Naphtali as a doe let loose who gives beautiful offspring. The term captures aesthetic excellence and pleasing form, whether in speech, appearance, or offspring. The brevity of usage makes precise definition challenging, but the semantic field clearly centers on visual or auditory beauty.

senses.1: Translations uniformly render this as 'beauty,' 'goodliness,' or 'attractiveness' (Spanish hermosura, French beauté, German Schönheit). The context in Genesis 49:21 links this beauty to Naphtali's 'words' or offspring, though textual ambiguities make the exact referent debated. The consistent cross-linguistic agreement confirms the core aesthetic sense of this rare noun.

gloss_terse: fairness, clearness, brightness (especially of the sky)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun describes the fair or clear state of the sky, appearing in Job 26:13 in a description of God's creative power. The verse speaks of how God's breath (or spirit) makes the sky fair—clearing away clouds or storm to reveal brightness. The term captures the visual quality of a cloudless, bright sky after disturbance. Most modern scholars accept this reading, though the Greek tradition suggests an alternative text. The word evokes the aesthetic transformation from darkness or storm to serene clarity.

senses.1: The English and Spanish translations ('became fair,' 'are beautiful') support the aesthetic sense of sky-clarity or brightness. French and German versions leave the word untranslated in Hebrew, perhaps indicating textual uncertainty. Job 26:13 uses this term to describe God's power to clear the heavens by his breath, making visible the beauty of the sky—part of a larger catalogue of divine creative acts.

gloss_terse: Shiphrah (personal name of a Hebrew midwife in Egypt)
gloss_readable: Shiphrah was one of two Hebrew midwives named in Exodus 1:15 who defied Pharaoh's command to kill male Hebrew infants. Along with Puah, she courageously preserved life despite royal decree, fearing God more than the king. Her name may derive from the root meaning 'beauty' or 'brightness,' suggesting either physical attractiveness or the beauty of her character. The Greek Septuagint renders her name as Sepphora (though this differs from Zipporah, Moses' wife). These midwives' civil disobedience represents one of the Bible's earliest examples of righteous resistance to unjust authority.

senses.1: All major translations simply transliterate the name as 'Shiphrah' or slight variants (Spanish Shifrah). The name occurs in the narrative context of Pharaoh's genocidal policy and the midwives' God-fearing refusal to comply, resulting in divine blessing upon their households. Shiphrah and Puah stand as heroes of the faith who risked their lives to preserve Israel's future generation.

gloss_terse: dawn, early morning, daybreak
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun appears in the book of Daniel, describing the time of dawn when King Darius rushed to the lions' den to check on Daniel. The word captures the first light of morning, that transitional moment when darkness yields to day. The reduplication in the Hebrew form suggests intensity or vividness—the brightness of breaking dawn. It evokes urgency and hope: Darius could not wait for full daylight but went 'at dawn' to see if Daniel's God had delivered him. The moment of dawn carries dramatic weight in the narrative.

senses.1: Most translations render this clearly as 'at dawn' or 'at daybreak' (Spanish al amanecer, French/German uncertain). The context in Daniel 6:19 emphasizes the king's anxious haste—he rose 'at first light' and hurried to the den. The dawn setting heightens the suspense and underscores Darius's sleepless concern for Daniel's fate.

gloss_terse: sheepfolds, sheep enclosures (dual form suggesting paired structures)
gloss_readable: This dual-form noun refers to sheepfolds or livestock enclosures, structures where shepherds penned their flocks for safety and rest. The word appears in Psalm 68:13 in a rhetorical question challenging those who stayed 'among the sheepfolds' rather than joining Israel's military campaigns. The term likely denotes the paired walls or double enclosures typical of ancient sheep pens. It may be related to mishpetayim, another term for similar structures. The sheepfolds represent safety and domesticity but also, in this context, cowardice—the comfortable place where some chose to remain rather than risk battle.

senses.1: English and Spanish consistently translate this as 'sheepfolds' or 'pens' (apriscos), while French offers 'watering trough' and German follows the English. The Psalm 68:13 context contrasts those who stayed comfortably 'among the sheepfolds' with warriors who engaged in battle, possibly echoing Deborah's rebuke in Judges 5:16 of those who remained 'among the sheep pens' hearing the whistling for the flocks.

gloss_terse: hooks, pegs, or ledges (architectural feature in Ezekiel's temple)
gloss_readable: This dual-form noun describes an architectural feature in Ezekiel's visionary temple, most commonly understood as hooks or pegs attached to the walls. Ancient versions suggest these were hook-shaped projections, possibly for hanging sacrificial animals during butchering. Alternative interpretations read the word as 'ledges' or 'edges,' referring to horizontal features along the walls. The term's rarity and technical nature have led to ongoing debate about its precise meaning. Whether hooks for meat or architectural ledges, the word describes structural details of the temple's sacrificial preparation areas.

senses.1: English and Spanish render this as 'hooks' (ganchos), following the Targum interpretation, while French again offers 'watering trough' and German leaves it untranslated. Ezekiel 40:43 describes these features as installed in the temple's interior, measuring a handbreadth and fastened all around, consistent with hooks for hanging sacrificial portions during priestly work.

gloss_terse: flood, deluge, overwhelming flow (literal or figurative)
gloss_readable: This noun describes a powerful flood or overwhelming surge of water, used both literally for natural floods and metaphorically for divine judgment or human calamity. The word appears in contexts of God's judgment sweeping away the wicked like a flood, or in Job describing the channels for the rain-flood. Isaiah uses the intensive form 'flood of wrath' to describe a temporary but fierce outpouring of divine anger. The term conveys unstoppable force, the kind of water that breaks through barriers and overwhelms everything in its path. Whether describing Noah's flood, invading armies, or emotional torrents, the image is one of inundating power.

senses.1: The phrase 'in a flood of wrath' (Isaiah 54:8) uses this term metaphorically for God's temporary anger that overwhelmed Israel in exile. While most translations render it as 'flood' or 'overflowing,' the French and German versions show some uncertainty with the text. The metaphor draws on the fearsome power of flash floods in the ancient Near East, where sudden storms could send walls of water through wadis, sweeping away everything.

gloss_terse: legs, lower legs (anatomical term)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun refers to the lower legs or shins, appearing in Daniel's vision of the great statue in Nebuchadnezzar's dream. The image's legs of iron represent a fourth kingdom, strong as iron but ultimately fragile when mixed with clay in the feet. The term specifically denotes the leg from knee to ankle, the weight-bearing portion that supports the entire structure. In the symbolic vision, these legs of iron convey both strength and the eventual fragility of human empire, standing strong but destined to fall when struck by God's kingdom-stone.

senses.1: The straightforward anatomical term is rendered as 'legs' across translations (Spanish piernas, French jambe). Daniel 2:33 describes the statue's legs of iron as part of the prophetic symbolism, representing a powerful kingdom that would crush and break all others—traditionally identified with Rome in Christian interpretation, or with the succession of empires in Jewish interpretation.

gloss_terse: be bound, tied on, fastened (possibly in error for 'be watched')
gloss_readable: This rare and disputed verb appears in Lamentations 1:14 describing Jerusalem's sins as bound together like a yoke upon her neck. The exact reading and root are uncertain; many scholars suggest emending to 'watch' based on the ancient versions, which would yield 'watch is kept upon my transgressions.' The Masoretic Text as it stands suggests binding or yoking together, presenting sin as cords woven into a yoke that burdens the neck. Either reading conveys the weight and constraint of accumulated sin—whether bound together as a heavy load or vigilantly observed by divine justice.

senses.1: English renders this as 'bound' while Spanish translates 'has been tied,' following the Masoretic Text's suggestion of binding or yoking. French and German leave it untranslated, reflecting scholarly uncertainty. The image in Lamentations 1:14 powerfully conveys sin's burden: transgressions intertwined by God's hand and placed as a yoke on Jerusalem's neck, making her strength fail under the weight.

gloss_terse: drink, beverage (figurative refreshment)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes drink or beverage, used both literally and figuratively in the Old Testament. In Proverbs, wisdom's instruction is described as 'drink to your bones'—refreshment and health for one's inner being. In the Psalms and Hosea, the term appears in contexts of mourning or deprivation, where tears become drink or where drink represents basic sustenance sought from false sources. The word captures the essential nature of liquid refreshment, but often with figurative overtones of spiritual or emotional satisfaction.

senses.1: The psalmist's lament in Psalm 102:9 declares 'my drink I have mingled with tears,' using this term for literal beverage made bitter by weeping. The Spanish translation 'my drink' and German 'my drinking' capture the straightforward reference to what one drinks. The context of mourning and divine discipline makes the drink a vehicle for expressing profound sorrow—every beverage tainted by tears.

gloss_terse: quietness, rest, tranquility
gloss_readable: This noun expresses the state of quietness or tranquility, appearing in God's promise to Solomon that he would be granted rest from enemies. The term is paired with 'peace' in 1 Chronicles 22:9, describing the conditions under which Solomon would build the temple—in contrast to David's life of warfare. Quietness suggests not merely the absence of conflict but the positive presence of calm, rest, and security. It evokes the settled conditions necessary for domestic prosperity and religious devotion, when weapons can be set aside for building projects.

senses.1: The phrase 'quietness and peace' in 1 Chronicles 22:9 uses this term to describe the conditions God promised Solomon's reign. French and German translations show some uncertainty, but the context clearly indicates restful conditions free from military threat. God tells David that Solomon's name means 'peace,' and He will give Israel 'quietness and peace' during his reign, enabling the temple construction that David's warfare-filled life could not accomplish.

gloss_terse: depressions, hollows, indentations (in a surface)
gloss_readable: This plural feminine noun describes depressions or hollows in a surface, specifically appearing in Leviticus 14:37 in the priestly diagnosis of house plague. The text describes how the priest examines wall depressions that appear greenish or reddish and seem deeper than the surface—signs of contaminating mildew or mold. The term denotes concave spots, indentations where the wall surface has eroded or deteriorated. These depressions distinguished serious structural contamination from surface staining, requiring priestly intervention and possible demolition.

senses.1: Translations consistently render this as 'depressions' or 'hollows' across languages (Spanish depresiones), describing the sunken spots in walls that indicated serious plague contamination. Leviticus 14:37 uses precise architectural terminology in the priestly manual for diagnosing house plague, with these depressions serving as diagnostic signs that the contamination had penetrated the wall's surface.

gloss_terse: frame, framework, casing (architectural feature for doors)
gloss_readable: This rare architectural term appears in the description of Solomon's palace, referring to the framework or casing around doorways and windows. The word likely denotes the structural framing that holds doors or the decorative casing that surrounds openings. In 1 Kings 7:5, the text describes architectural features 'frame against frame' in three rows, suggesting a repeated pattern of framed openings in the palace structure. The term represents the technical vocabulary of ancient Near Eastern architecture, preserving details of royal construction techniques.

senses.1: English and Spanish render this as 'frame' or 'framed,' describing architectural features in Solomon's palace. The context in 1 Kings 7:5 speaks of doors and doorposts that were 'square in their frames,' with frame facing frame in three tiers—likely describing a colonnade or gallery with multiple framed openings in parallel rows, demonstrating the palace's sophisticated architectural design.

gloss_terse: ogle, glance provocatively, cast flirtatious looks
gloss_readable: This Piel verb describes the provocative eye movements of women seeking to attract attention through seductive glances. Isaiah uses it in his indictment of Jerusalem's wealthy women who walk with 'ogling eyes'—part of their overall haughty, attention-seeking behavior. The root suggests deliberate eye movement calculated to entice or seduce, distinct from modest gaze. Cognate languages support the sense of looking about in a calculating or flirtatious manner. The term captures not just seeing but the deliberate use of eye contact as a social and sexual signal.

senses.1: Isaiah 3:16 condemns the daughters of Zion for 'walking and ogling with their eyes,' part of a larger rebuke of their pride and seductive behavior. Spanish captures the sense with 'seducing with,' while French and German leave it untranslated, perhaps due to its unusual nature. The ogling represents calculated sensuality—using eye movement as a tool of enticement, part of the social display that Isaiah declares will be judged by humiliation.

gloss_terse: escape, survive, get away
gloss_readable: This verb describes escaping from danger or surviving destruction, appearing in Joshua's account of the conquest of the five Amorite kings. After Israel's great slaughter of enemy forces, the few who survived 'escaped' to fortified cities for refuge. The root conveys the sense of fleeing or slipping away from destruction, managing to survive when most perished. Cognate languages suggest connotations of being startled and fleeing in terror, running away like a frightened animal. The term captures both the act of escape and the survivor's status among the fallen.

senses.1: Joshua 10:20 describes how after Israel's massive slaughter of the Amorite armies, 'those who survived' managed to reach their fortified cities. The English and Spanish translations ('survived,' sobrevivieron) emphasize the outcome—making it through the destruction alive. The context highlights the completeness of Israel's victory, with only remnants escaping to walled cities while the majority fell in battle.

gloss_terse: stylus, marking tool (for working wood)
gloss_readable: This rare noun denotes a marking tool or stylus used in woodworking, appearing in Isaiah's satire of idol-making. The craftsman uses this tool to mark out or design the wooden figure before carving it. Ancient versions suggest it was an engraving or marking implement, possibly related to the precious stone sardius (used in gem-cutting), though the connection is uncertain. The term represents the technical vocabulary of craftsmanship, highlighting the ironic process by which humans create gods with simple tools—marking, measuring, and shaping dead wood into objects of worship.

senses.1: Isaiah 44:13 describes the carpenter who 'marks it out with a stylus,' part of the detailed satire of idol-making that emphasizes the absurdity of worshiping what human hands craft from ordinary materials. Spanish translates 'with pencil,' capturing the marking function. The stylus represents the planning stage of idol-making, where the craftsman designs on wood the figure he will worship—underscoring the human origin of supposedly divine objects.

gloss_terse: loosen, set free, release from bonds
gloss_readable: This verb means to loosen, release, or set free from constraint. The root appears in contexts of physical liberation or, metaphorically, of God releasing forces like thunder. In Jeremiah 15:11, the verb appears in a textually difficult passage where God promises to 'free' or 'strengthen' Jeremiah (the Hebrew text has variant readings). The basic sense involves undoing bindings or constraints, whether literal ropes or figurative restrictions. Cognate languages support meanings of loosing, releasing, and even the sense of dedicating or opening something for use.

senses.1: Jeremiah 15:11 contains textual difficulties, with the written (Ketiv) and read (Qere) texts differing. The Qere suggests 'I will set you free' or 'loose you,' while interpretations vary between liberation and strengthening. Spanish offers 'I freed you,' following the liberation sense, while French and German leave it transliterated, acknowledging the textual uncertainty. The broader context of God's promise to Jeremiah supports either nuance—whether freed from opposition or strengthened for his prophetic mission.

gloss_terse: rows, vine-rows (agricultural term)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun describes rows of cultivated plants, particularly olive trees or grapevines planted in organized lines for agricultural production. The term appears in Job's critique of the wicked who oppress workers laboring among the olive rows, and possibly in Jeremiah's judgment oracle about invading Israel's vine-rows. The word represents agricultural organization—the careful arrangement of perennial crops in parallel rows for efficient cultivation and harvest. It evokes the ordered vineyard or olive grove, where workers toiled between the rows but enjoyed none of the fruit.

senses.1: The evidence shows uncertainty about this term's precise reference. Job 24:11 likely describes workers who 'make oil among the rows' of olive trees, while Jeremiah 5:10 possibly refers to enemy forces invading 'among her vine-rows' (if the text is emended). Spanish translates 'to her walls,' showing the interpretive difficulty. The agricultural sense of organized plant rows seems clear from comparative evidence, though the specific crop varies by context.

gloss_terse: bracelets, ornamental arm bands
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes bracelets or ornamental bands worn on the arms or wrists, appearing in Isaiah's catalogue of women's finery. These were jewelry items that displayed wealth and fashion, part of the elaborate ornamentation worn by Jerusalem's elite women. The term may relate to roots suggesting chains or binding, as bracelets encircle the arm. In ancient Near Eastern culture, such jewelry carried social significance—indicating status, wealth, and marriageability. Isaiah's list condemns not the jewelry itself but the pride and luxury-seeking it represents in a society neglecting justice.

senses.1: Isaiah 3:19 includes 'the bracelets' in an extensive list of luxury items God will remove from Jerusalem's proud women in judgment. Spanish translates 'the bracelets' (las pulseras), confirming the jewelry identification. The list encompasses earrings, nose rings, robes, perfumes, and multiple ornamental items—all symbols of the women's privileged status that Isaiah declares will be stripped away, replaced by shame and mourning.

gloss_terse: Sharuhen (place name: city in Simeon's territory)
gloss_readable: Sharuhen was a city allotted to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory, mentioned in the boundary descriptions of Joshua 19. The location is uncertain, though some scholars identify it with an Egyptian site name Sha-ru-ha-na. The Septuagint's unusual rendering ('their fields') may reflect textual confusion or an alternative reading. Like many Simeonite settlements, Sharuhen was located in the Negev region of southern Judah. The city represents one of the towns Simeon inherited when their tribal allotment was carved from Judah's portion, since 'Judah's portion was too large for them.'

senses.1: Joshua 19:6 lists Sharuhen among the thirteen cities given to Simeon. English and Spanish simply transliterate the name (Sharuhén), while French follows suit. The city appears in a list alongside Bethlehem, Hormah, and other southern settlements. Some scholars connect this site with Shilhim (Joshua 15:32) or Shaaraim (1 Chronicles 4:31), suggesting these may be variant names for the same location.

gloss_terse: Sharonite (gentilic: person from Sharon region)
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective identifies someone as being from Sharon, the fertile coastal plain between Joppa and Mount Carmel. The term appears in 1 Chronicles 27:29 in reference to Shitrai the Sharonite, who supervised David's cattle that grazed in Sharon. The Sharon plain was renowned for its fertility and pasturage, making it ideal for livestock. The designation 'Sharonite' indicates geographic origin and possibly suggests expertise in managing herds in that rich pastoral region. The plain of Sharon's beauty and fruitfulness made it a biblical image of splendor and divine blessing.

senses.1: The designation 'the Sharonite' (1 Chronicles 27:29) identifies Shitrai as a man from the Sharon region who oversaw the king's herds pasturing in that fertile plain. Spanish renders this as 'the Saronite,' following the transliteration pattern. The context shows David's sophisticated administration, with different officials managing herds in different regions—Shitrai handling the Sharon cattle while another managed those in the valleys.

gloss_terse: choice branches, vine tendrils (of grapevines)
gloss_readable: This masculine plural noun refers to the choice branches or tendrils of grapevines, appearing in Isaiah's lament over Moab's destroyed vineyards. These branches represent the productive, fruit-bearing parts of the vine that spread outward, or possibly the choice clusters that hang from them. The term may derive from the red color of ripened grapes or autumn leaves. In Isaiah 16:8, the 'choice branches' of Heshbon's vines once reached far and spread out abundantly, symbolizing Moab's agricultural prosperity. Their breaking represents economic and national devastation.

senses.1: Isaiah 16:8 mourns that 'its choice branches' have been broken—referring to the famous vines of Heshbon whose branches once reached to Jazer and spread across the desert, even crossing the sea. Spanish translates 'its tendrils' (sus sarmientos), emphasizing the vine-branches. The image captures agricultural destruction: the spreading, productive branches that once testified to Moab's wealth now lie broken and trampled by conquerors.

gloss_terse: K reading uncertain: possibly 'I vexed/troubled you' or scribal variant
gloss_readable: This entry represents the Ketiv (written) text of Jeremiah 15:11, which differs from the Qere (read) text. The written form appears to come from a root meaning to vex, trouble, or possibly to strengthen, but the textual transmission is disputed. The Ketiv suggests 'I vexed you' or 'I ruled/strengthened you,' while the Qere reads 'I freed you.' Most English translations follow the Qere or emend the text. The variant reflects scribal uncertainty about a difficult prophetic oracle where God assures Jeremiah of divine intervention. The confusion highlights the challenges of preserving ancient Hebrew texts through centuries of hand-copying.

senses.1: The Spanish translation offers 'I freed you' (following Qere), while French and German leave it untranslated in Hebrew brackets, acknowledging the textual problem. The context involves God's promise to Jeremiah regarding his prophetic mission and the treatment he would receive from enemies. The Ketiv may represent an early textual error or an alternative tradition, but most interpreters follow the Qere reading that promises liberation rather than affliction.

gloss_terse: incision, cut, gash (in flesh)
gloss_readable: This masculine noun denotes a deliberate cut or incision made in flesh, appearing in Levitical laws prohibiting pagan mourning practices. Leviticus 19:28 forbids making 'cuts in your flesh for the dead,' referring to the ancient Near Eastern custom of ritual self-laceration during mourning or religious devotion. These incisions were marks of grief or cultic identification, common among Israel's neighbors but prohibited in Torah as incompatible with covenant identity. The practice suggested that the body could be manipulated to appease gods or honor the dead, conflicting with Israel's understanding of the body as God's creation.

senses.1: The prohibition 'you shall not make a cutting in your flesh' (Leviticus 19:28) uses this term for the ritual gashes forbidden to Israelites. English and Spanish translate as 'cutting' or 'incision,' capturing the deliberate act of slashing flesh. The context pairs this prohibition with tattoos, both representing permanent body modifications associated with pagan religious practices. The law establishes the body's sanctity and Israel's distinctiveness from surrounding peoples.

gloss_terse: incision, cut, gash (variant form)
gloss_readable: This feminine form serves as a variant of the previous entry, denoting the same practice of ritual cutting or self-laceration. It appears in Leviticus 21:5 in priestly regulations specifically prohibiting priests from making 'cuts in their flesh' as part of mourning practices. While the general Israelite population faced this prohibition in Leviticus 19, the repetition for priests emphasizes their special sanctity and the importance of avoiding pagan-influenced mourning customs. The term describes the same incisions or gashes cut into flesh during mourning, practices firmly rejected in Israel's holiness code.

senses.1: Leviticus 21:5 specifically commands priests not to 'make cuts in their flesh,' using this variant form of the incision term. English and Spanish translate as 'a cut' or 'incision,' identical to the previous entry's meaning. The priestly code's special attention to this prohibition reflects the heightened holiness requirements for those serving in the sanctuary, where bodily integrity and separation from pagan mourning customs was especially crucial.

gloss_terse: Sharai (personal name of a man with a foreign wife during Ezra's reforms)
gloss_readable: Sharai appears among the list of Israelite men who had married foreign women during the exile and agreed to divorce them during Ezra's reforms. The name occurs in Ezra 10:40 in the catalogue of those who had intermarried contrary to the law's prohibition. The Greek versions offer various transliterations (Sariou, Saroue, Saroua) showing uncertainty in vocalization. Like others in this list, Sharai represents the postexilic community's struggle with maintaining ethnic and religious boundaries, ultimately yielding to the demand for separation from foreign wives to preserve covenant faithfulness.

senses.1: Ezra 10:40 lists Sharai among approximately 110 men identified as having foreign wives whom they agreed to send away. Most translations simply transliterate the name. The inclusion in this list marks Sharai as part of the community that responded to Ezra's call for repentance, though the personal cost of dissolving marriages and separating from children made this one of the Bible's most ethically troubling reform movements.

gloss_terse: javelin, lance, or possibly coat of armor (weapon or protective gear)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun appears in Job's description of Leviathan's invincibility, listing weapons that cannot pierce the creature. The term likely denotes either a javelin or lance (a throwing or thrusting spear), or possibly body armor (corselet or breastplate), based on variant manuscript traditions. The Hebrew text suggests a weapon in a list including sword, spear, and dart, but the Greek and Latin versions read 'breastplate,' suggesting a different vocalization. Either reading emphasizes Leviathan's imperviousness—whether weapons bounce off or armor proves useless against him.

senses.1: Job 41:26 declares that various weapons—sword, spear, dart, 'and javelin'—cannot make Leviathan flee. Spanish translates 'coat of armor' (coraza), following the Vulgate's reading, while French and German leave it untranslated. The context emphasizes Leviathan's supremacy over human military technology: conventional weapons that work against normal creatures prove worthless against this symbol of untamable chaos.

gloss_terse: combed, carded (processed flax ready for weaving)
gloss_readable: This feminine plural adjective describes flax that has been combed or carded—processed through the preparatory stages of separating and aligning the fibers for spinning and weaving. Isaiah uses the term in his judgment oracle against Egypt, where workers in 'combed flax' will be dismayed when Egypt's economic infrastructure collapses. The word captures a specific stage in textile production, after the flax has been retted and broken but before spinning. It represents skilled labor and a significant sector of Egypt's economy, which depended on linen production. The combed flax workers' dismay symbolizes Egypt's comprehensive economic devastation.

senses.1: Isaiah 19:9 prophesies that 'workers in combed flax' will be in despair when Egypt's Nile-based economy fails. Spanish translates 'combed,' capturing the textile-processing sense, while French and German leave it untranslated, perhaps due to the technical specificity. The image is of Egypt's linen industry—from flax cultivation through processing to weaving—collapsing when divine judgment strikes, leaving specialized craftspeople without livelihood.

gloss_terse: sinews, muscles (anatomical term for strong tissues)
gloss_readable: This masculine plural noun denotes the sinews or muscles, the strong fibrous tissues that enable bodily movement and strength. The term appears in God's description of Behemoth in Job 40:16, highlighting the creature's extraordinary physical power. The parallel structure pairs this term with 'loins,' emphasizing Behemoth's massive muscular structure. Sinews represent the source of animal and human strength, the tissues that connect bone to muscle and generate force. In Behemoth's case, the sinews of his belly concentrate tremendous power, making him an unmatched example of God's creative might.

senses.1: Job 40:16 declares that Behemoth's 'power is in the muscles of his belly,' parallel to 'his strength is in his loins.' Spanish translates 'in the muscles of,' while French and German show uncertainty. The anatomical language emphasizes Behemoth's core strength—the massive musculature of his abdomen that enables his powerful movements. God's point is that the creature's strength far exceeds human capacity, demonstrating divine creative power beyond human comprehension or control.

gloss_terse: twist, entangle, interweave (especially of paths or ways)
gloss_readable: This Piel verb means to twist together, entangle, or interweave, appearing in Jeremiah's accusation against faithless Israel. The prophet uses the image of a swift young camel 'entangling her ways'—running about in confused, crisscrossing paths during mating season, leaving tracks that loop and twist everywhere. The verb captures chaotic, purposeless movement that weaves back and forth without clear direction. It conveys both physical entanglement and metaphorical confusion—Israel's spiritual promiscuity compared to an animal in heat, rushing frantically in all directions seeking satisfaction.

senses.1: Jeremiah 2:23 describes faithless Israel as 'a swift camel entangling her ways,' using this term for the confused, crisscrossing tracks left by the frantic animal. Spanish translates 'crossing' or 'intertwining' (entrecruza), capturing the weaving-together sense. The image is of irrational, driven behavior—like an animal in heat that runs wildly in every direction, leaving a tangled maze of footprints. Israel's pursuit of other gods mirrors this frenzied, shameless searching.

gloss_terse: K variant reading: possibly 'walls' or 'ramparts' (textual variant for 'fields')
gloss_readable: This entry represents the Ketiv reading in Jeremiah 31:40, where the written text differs from the Qere (read) form. The Qere reads 'fields,' the standard word for cultivated lands, while the Ketiv presents an uncertain form. The context describes the rebuilt Jerusalem's extended boundaries, encompassing various locations including fields or possibly ramparts. The textual variant reflects scribal uncertainty about this geographical description in Jeremiah's prophecy of restoration. Most modern translations follow the Qere reading of 'fields,' treating the Ketiv as a scribal error or dialectal variant.

senses.1: The geographic description in Jeremiah 31:40 lists areas that will be holy to the Lord when Jerusalem is rebuilt. The Ketiv suggests 'walls' or 'ramparts,' while the Qere reads 'fields,' with most translations following the latter. French and German leave it in Hebrew brackets, acknowledging the textual problem. The broader context describes Jerusalem's expanded sacred boundaries, encompassing even areas previously considered unclean—the valley of corpses and ashes transformed into holy ground.

gloss_terse: Saraph (personal name of a Judahite who 'ruled in Moab')
gloss_readable: Saraph appears in 1 Chronicles 4:22 as a descendant of Judah, noted for having 'ruled in Moab.' The brief reference suggests he exercised authority over Moabite territory, possibly as a governor during Israel's dominance over Moab under David or Solomon. His name derives from the root meaning 'burn,' the same root that gives us 'seraphim.' The terse genealogical note leaves much uncertain—whether his rule was administrative, military, or represented intermarriage and settlement. The text notes these are 'ancient records,' suggesting the chronicler drew from old sources whose full context was already partially lost.

senses.1: The genealogical note in 1 Chronicles 4:22 simply states that Saraph 'ruled in Moab,' with most translations (Spanish: Saraf) offering transliteration. The unusual detail about Moabite rule stands out in the genealogy, hinting at Judahite expansion or influence over neighboring peoples during the early monarchy. The name and his connection to Moab receive no further biblical development, leaving Saraph as one of Scripture's many briefly-mentioned figures whose fuller story remains lost.

gloss_terse: sorrel (color description of horses: reddish-brown)
gloss_readable: This masculine plural adjective describes the color of horses in Zechariah's night vision, most commonly understood as 'sorrel'—a reddish-brown or chestnut hue. The term appears in a list of horse colors: red, sorrel, and white. The root may relate to redness or the color of fine grapes, suggesting a brownish-red or rust color. In ancient Near Eastern context, horse colors carried symbolic significance in military and visionary contexts. These variously colored horses pull chariots in Zechariah's vision of divine agents patrolling the earth, with the color distinctions possibly indicating different functions or jurisdictions.

senses.1: Zechariah 1:8 describes the prophet's vision of horses with three color designations: 'red, sorrel, and white.' Spanish translates 'chestnut' or 'bay' (alazanes), confirming the brownish-red horse color, while French offers simply 'red.' The vision presents these colored horses among the myrtle trees with riders who patrol the earth as the Lord's scouts. The color distinction serves the vision's symbolic framework, though interpreters debate whether specific theological meanings attach to each color.

gloss_terse: choice vine, noble vine (superior grape variety)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes a choice or noble vine, a superior variety of grape known for quality fruit. The term appears in Jacob's blessing upon Judah in Genesis 49:11, in poetic imagery of abundance and royalty. The 'choice vine' represents valuable agricultural stock, the kind of vine a wealthy landowner would cultivate for premium wine production. In the prophetic imagery, Judah's abundance will be so great that he can afford to tie his donkey to a choice vine—treating valuable property casually because of overwhelming prosperity. The term emphasizes quality and value, distinguishing superior vines from common varieties.

senses.1: Genesis 49:11 pictures Judah tying his donkey 'to the choice vine,' part of vivid imagery of wine abundance during Judah's reign. English and Spanish translate 'choice vine' or 'noble vine' (cepa), emphasizing the quality designation. The image conveys messianic abundance: royal prosperity so great that even valuable grapevines serve utilitarian purposes like hitching posts, and wine flows so freely that one washes clothes in it—a vision of Eden-like fruitfulness under Judah's scepter.

gloss_terse: Sharar (personal name: father of one of David's mighty men)
gloss_readable: Sharar appears in 2 Samuel 23:33 as the father of Ahiam, one of David's elite warriors known as 'the Thirty.' The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:35 gives the name as Sacar (or Sachar), suggesting textual variation or possibly two names for the same person. Personal names in the lists of David's mighty men often show such variation between Samuel and Chronicles. Sharar himself receives no other biblical mention; his significance derives entirely from his son's place among David's honored combat veterans who performed extraordinary military feats.

senses.1: The designation 'Ahiam son of Sharar' (2 Samuel 23:33) identifies one of David's elite Thirty warriors by patronymic. All major translations simply transliterate the name (Sharar). His inclusion in this prestigious list honors his son's military service and places Sharar's family among the heroes of David's reign. The slight variation with Chronicles (Sacar) reflects the common textual fluidity in personal names transmitted through centuries of hand-copying.

gloss_terse: navel, navel-string, or possibly body/belly (anatomical term)
gloss_readable: This masculine noun denotes the navel or navel-string (umbilical cord), appearing in Ezekiel's allegory of Jerusalem's origins and in wisdom literature. In Ezekiel 16:4, God speaks of Jerusalem's birth when 'your navel-string was not cut,' part of vivid imagery describing Israel's abandoned, unwashed infancy before God's adoption. The term may extend metaphorically to mean the body's center or the belly generally. In disputed passages in Proverbs and Song of Songs, translations vary between 'navel,' 'body,' and even 'vulva,' reflecting interpretive challenges with intimate anatomical vocabulary.

senses.1: Song of Songs 7:2 uses this term in the lover's description of his beloved's body, translated as 'navel' or 'body's center,' though some suggest euphemistic reference to female anatomy. Spanish translates 'your navel,' while French offers 'your navel.' The context describes physical beauty in highly metaphorical language, where various body parts receive poetic comparison to landscape features. Whether specifically the navel or more broadly the belly/body center, the term fits the passage's celebratory, sensual description.
